stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman at 27 weeks gestation. She is in her second pregnancy, BMI 28 at booking, with a previous baby of 4100 g at 39 weeks. She had no anomalies on the 20-week scan. She is asymptomatic. Her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test results have just returned.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height 28 cm; symphysis-fundal height appropriate; fetal heart rate 144 bpm
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.3 mmol/L, 1 hour 9.4 mmol/L, 2 hour 7.8 mmol/L; HbA1c at booking 5.4%; urine ketones negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that all values are normal; continue routine antenatal care and rescreen at 35 weeks if clinically indicated
options.rationale: Fasting 5.3 and 1 hour 9.4 mmol/L both meet ADIPS thresholds for GDM; reassurance misses the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS Guideline on GDM)

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily and refer to a diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic for review within 1 week
options.rationale: First-line for GDM is medical nutrition therapy and self-monitoring of glucose; metformin is added if glycaemic targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks of lifestyle measures. (Source: ADIPS Guideline on GDM)

options.text: Diagnose GDM; refer to a diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic for medical nutrition therapy and home glucose monitoring
options.rationale: Fasting 5.3 (threshold above 5.1) and 1 hour 9.4 (threshold above 10.0 not met but fasting alone is diagnostic) meet ADIPS GDM diagnostic criteria; first-line is multidisciplinary lifestyle support and home glucose monitoring. (Source: ADIPS Guideline on GDM)

options.text: Commence insulin glargine 10 units nocte; arrange home glucose monitoring with 4 daily checks
options.rationale: Insulin is reserved for failure of lifestyle and oral hypoglycaemics to meet glycaemic targets over 1 to 2 weeks; routine initial insulin is not standard. (Source: ADIPS Guideline on GDM)

options.text: Repeat the 75 g OGTT in 2 weeks for confirmation; commence aspirin 100 mg daily in the interim for pregnancy risk
options.rationale: GDM does not require repeat OGTT for confirmation; aspirin is for high pre-eclampsia risk, not GDM. (Source: ADIPS Guideline on GDM)

explanation.summary: Australian ADIPS GDM diagnostic thresholds on a 75 g OGTT are fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L or above, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or above, OR 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or above; one value is sufficient for diagnosis. Universal screening is performed at 24 to 28 weeks; women with risk factors (BMI 30 or above, previous GDM, family history, ethnicity, previous macrosomia) may be screened earlier. First-line management is medical nutrition therapy, physical activity and self-monitoring of glucose; pharmacotherapy with metformin or insulin is added if targets are not met within 1 to 2 weeks.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds: fasting above 5.0, 1 hour above 9.9, 2 hour above 8.4
First line is lifestyle plus self-monitoring
Pharmacotherapy if targets unmet at 1 to 2 weeks
explanation.pearls: Postpartum 75 g OGTT at 6 to 12 weeks is recommended for all GDM women; up to 50 percent develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years.

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia with magnesium sulfate prophylaxis
stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 35 weeks gestation presents to the labour ward with severe occipital headache, blurred vision and right upper quadrant pain. She has been booked under midwifery-led care and has had unremarkable antenatal results until this presentation.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 178/115 (confirmed on 2 readings 15 min apart), HR 88, T 36.8, SpO2 97 percent
data_table.Examination: Hyperreflexia with 4 beats clonus bilateral; severe occipital headache; visual blurring; right upper quadrant tenderness; oedema lower limbs; fetal heart 140 bpm
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 3+ protein, PCR 0.42 g/mmol; platelets 95 x10^9/L; ALT 178 U/L; LDH 850; creatinine 92; bilirubin normal; FBC otherwise normal; haptoglobin normal; fetal CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion, with intravenous labetalol for blood pressure control
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia (BP 160/110 or higher with proteinuria, or with severe features: headache, visual disturbance, RUQ pain, hyperreflexia, low platelets, ALT over twice the upper limit) requires immediate IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prevention (4 g loading over 20 min, then 1 g/hour infusion for 24 h or 24 h postpartum), and BP control (IV labetalol or hydralazine, target SBP 140-150 / DBP 90-100). Plan for delivery after stabilisation. (Source: RANZCOG; SOMANZ)

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 11.4 mg for fetal lung maturity and observe blood pressure overnight without antihypertensive therapy
options.rationale: Steroids alone do not address eclampsia risk; magnesium sulfate is the priority seizure prevention. (Source: SOMANZ)

options.text: Administer oral nifedipine 10 mg immediate release and observe with hourly blood pressure for 6 hours before any further intervention
options.rationale: Oral nifedipine is appropriate for non-severe hypertension; severe pre-eclampsia requires IV agents and magnesium. (Source: SOMANZ)

options.text: Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg to manage the oedema and reduce blood pressure before any other targeted intervention today
options.rationale: Loop diuretics are contraindicated in pre-eclampsia (reduce placental perfusion) unless pulmonary oedema is present. (Source: SOMANZ)

options.text: Administer oral aspirin 150 mg daily as first-line preventive treatment for pre-eclampsia at this gestation today
options.rationale: Aspirin is preventive (initiated before 16 weeks for high-risk women) not for treating established severe pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia has BP 160/110 or higher, proteinuria PCR 0.30 g/mmol or higher, AND/OR severe features (headache, visual symptoms, RUQ pain, low platelets below 100, ALT over twice ULN, creatinine over 90, hyperreflexia, pulmonary oedema). Management: magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis (4 g loading plus 1 g/hour for 24 hours), IV labetalol or hydralazine for BP, fluid restriction (80 mL/hour total), plan delivery after maternal stabilisation. Magnesium toxicity monitored by deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output; calcium gluconate is the antidote. Betamethasone for fetal lung maturity if delivery before 34 weeks. Definitive treatment is delivery.
key_points: Severe features = headache, visual change, RUQ pain, hyperreflexia, low platelets, raised ALT
Magnesium sulfate 4 g load plus 1 g/hour for 24 hours (seizure prophylaxis)
IV labetalol or hydralazine for BP control
Calcium gluconate is the magnesium antidote
explanation.pearls: The MAGPIE trial showed magnesium sulfate halves the risk of eclamptic seizures in pre-eclampsia (NNT around 91 for severe pre-eclampsia, NNT around 36 for imminent eclampsia); it remains underused outside specialist units despite this strong evidence.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is reviewed on day 4 after an emergency caesarean for failure to progress with prolonged rupture of membranes. She reports increasing lower abdominal pain, malodorous lochia and rigors since this morning. She has no penicillin allergy. The wound is clean and dry; her hospital documented an estimated blood loss of 700 mL with no transfusion.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen suprapubic tenderness, uterus 18 cm above pubis (subinvoluted), foul-smelling lochia
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.5 x10^9/L, CRP 142 mg/L, Hb 96 g/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, blood and high vaginal cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Septic-range temperature and tachycardia after caesarean require IV therapy; oral cover is insufficient for moderate to severe endometritis. (Source: eTG)

options.text: Intravenous ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole until afebrile for 24 hours
options.rationale: AU eTG first-line for moderate to severe postpartum endometritis is ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole until afebrile for 24 to 48 hours, then no oral step-down is typically needed. (Source: eTG)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam with infectious diseases consult overnight
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum carbapenem-sparing cover is reserved for failure of first-line therapy or known resistant organisms; it is not first-line. (Source: eTG)

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin and oral metronidazole with discharge once two doses given
options.rationale: Cefazolin monotherapy does not cover anaerobes adequately and discharge before clinical improvement risks deterioration. (Source: eTG)

options.text: Single dose intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g with planned obstetric outpatient follow-up tomorrow
options.rationale: Single-dose therapy is inadequate for established polymicrobial endometritis; inpatient combination therapy is required. (Source: eTG)

explanation.summary: Postpartum endometritis affects up to 6 percent of caesareans (higher with prolonged ROM, intrapartum chorio, multiple vaginal examinations). It is polymicrobial - aerobic and anaerobic Gram-positives and Gram-negatives - so AU first-line combination therapy is ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole IV. Clinical improvement is expected within 48 to 72 hours; persistence beyond that warrants imaging to exclude retained products, pelvic abscess, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis or wound infection.
key_points: Triad: fever, foul lochia, uterine tenderness after delivery.
Polymicrobial - cover Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobes.
AU first-line: ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole IV.
Continue until afebrile 24 to 48 hours; oral step-down is usually not needed.
No improvement at 48 to 72 hours = image for retained products or abscess.
explanation.pearls: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis presents as ongoing fever despite appropriate antibiotics for endometritis; CT pelvis with venous-phase contrast and therapeutic anticoagulation is diagnostic and therapeutic.

stem: You are the obstetrics registrar in delivery suite. A 33-year-old G2P1 at 36+4 weeks ruptures membranes spontaneously at home and notes a small amount of bright red bleeding immediately. On arrival 30 minutes later her CTG shows a sinusoidal pattern with fetal heart rate 130 bpm. Vaginal examination shows clear blood-stained liquor. Her booking morphology scan at 20 weeks reported a low-lying placenta but no follow-up scan was performed. Maternal observations are stable and she is not in labour.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 116/72, HR 88; FHR 130 bpm, sinusoidal trace, no decelerations yet
data_table.Examination: Cervix 2 cm dilated, head 0 station, blood-stained clear liquor
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118; group and hold sent; Kleihauer pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Allow expectant management with continuous CTG and oxygen via face mask at 10 L/min
options.rationale: Vasa praevia exsanguinates the fetus within minutes; expectant management is contraindicated when the CTG shows sinusoidal pattern with bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG APH Guideline)

options.text: Urgent transabdominal ultrasound to identify vasa praevia and placental site before delivery
options.rationale: Sinusoidal CTG and bleeding post-SROM is presumptive vasa praevia; delaying delivery for confirmatory imaging risks fetal exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG APH Guideline)

options.text: Category 1 emergency caesarean section with neonatal team in attendance for resuscitation
options.rationale: Sinusoidal CTG with vaginal bleeding immediately after SROM in a woman with previously low-lying placenta is classic vasa praevia until proven otherwise; fetal exsanguination is rapid and immediate caesarean is required. (Source: RANZCOG APH Guideline)

options.text: Augment labour with oxytocin and aim for rapid vaginal delivery within the next hour
options.rationale: Augmentation of labour with fetal exsanguination from suspected vasa praevia delays definitive control of haemorrhage; immediate caesarean is required. (Source: RANZCOG APH Guideline)

options.text: Send urgent fetal Kleihauer test on maternal blood to confirm fetal origin before delivery
options.rationale: Apt or Kleihauer testing to identify fetal blood is too slow when CTG already shows sinusoidal pattern indicating active fetal blood loss. (Source: RANZCOG APH Guideline)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia describes fetal vessels (either from a velamentous cord or between placental lobes in a succenturiate placenta) running through the membranes over the cervix, vulnerable to rupture at SROM and resulting in catastrophic fetal exsanguination. Diagnosis is ideally made antenatally via transvaginal Doppler in women with risk factors (low-lying placenta, succenturiate lobe, velamentous insertion, multiple pregnancy, IVF). Antenatal diagnosis allows planned caesarean at 35 to 36 weeks with corticosteroids. Acute presentation (SROM + vaginal bleeding + sinusoidal CTG) requires Category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes; fetal mortality without immediate delivery exceeds 50%. Apt test or Kleihauer can confirm fetal origin retrospectively but should not delay delivery.
key_points: Vasa praevia: fetal vessels over the cervix, exsanguination at SROM
Risk factors: velamentous insertion, succenturiate lobe, IVF, multiple, low-lying placenta
Antenatal Doppler diagnosis enables planned CS at 35-36 weeks
Acute presentation: sinusoidal CTG + bleeding + SROM = Cat 1 CS
explanation.pearls: Sinusoidal CTG with fetal anaemia shows a smooth sine wave of 5 to 15 bpm amplitude at 2 to 5 cycles/min and is essentially pathognomonic of acute fetal blood loss until proven otherwise.
